---
title: "Lab 1 — Templates and limits"
subtitle: "Day One · 30 min"
---

Three short comparisons. In each one you change one thing and put the two results side by side, so you can see the difference for yourself. You are not timing anything or counting edits. You are looking. It all runs on a synthetic case, and none of it uses a real patient.

::: {.session-meta}
Time
:   30 minutes: same case, two prompts 12; ask for what it cannot know 8; one question, two ways of answering 5; debrief 5

Slides
:   [Open the deck](../slides/lab1-templates-and-limits.qmd): the same lab, one step to a slide, with the pictures.

Uses
:   [Case A](../reference/case-cards.qmd#case-a), plus the question from [Case C](../reference/case-cards.qmd#case-c) as a default in part 3

You leave with
:   Two drafts of one note and your own tick count for each; a saved, deliberately unreliable answer you have run through the three-question check (Lab 3 reuses it); a first look at what a source you can open lets you check; and one prompt to bring to Day Two.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## On the call
You need three tabs: the call, the slides (your instructor pastes the link in the chat), and your general assistant, signed in. Copy each prompt from its slide with the Copy prompt button; your instructor pastes it in the chat too. Part 3 adds one more tab for your second option, for five minutes: a literature-grounded tool, your assistant's search or citation mode, or a literature search such as PubMed ([Module 3](m3-choosing-tools.qmd#second-option)). Any of the three will do, and no special account is needed. This page is the take-home version: every step again, to redo at your own pace.
:::

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Case A is the only patient in this lab
No patient identifiers into a consumer AI tool. Ever. Full stop. Do not swap in a real patient, even to save time.
:::

## 1. Same case, two prompts [12 min]{.time} {#part-1}

**The one change: the prompt.** [Module 2](m2-prompting.qmd) argued that a prompt built on the four-part framework gets you closer to the note you would write. Here you see it for yourself. Same case, same tool, a new chat for each, and the first draft only. Then you put the two drafts side by side.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    F1["Case A facts"] --> A["Prompt A<br/>one line"]
    F2["Case A facts"] --> B["Prompt B<br/>four parts"]
    A --> DA["Draft A"]
    B --> DB["Draft B"]
    DA --> C["Six checks<br/>against the card"]
    DB --> C
    classDef same fill:#F1F5F9,stroke:#64748B,color:#0F172A
    classDef change fill:#EEF2FF,stroke:#4F46E5,stroke-width:3px,color:#0F172A
    classDef out fill:#CCFBF1,stroke:#14B8A6,color:#0F172A
    class F1,F2 same
    class A,B change
    class DA,DB,C out
```

### The facts {#the-facts}

Copy this block. Both rounds use it. It is [Case A](../reference/case-cards.qmd#case-a), a fictional patient.

```text
CASE A (fictional patient): primary care clinic, follow-up visit, 6 weeks after starting treatment
- 52 M. Hypertension diagnosed 2 months ago. Started amlodipine 5 mg once daily 6 weeks ago.
- Says the headaches (mostly mornings) are less frequent. New since starting amlodipine: ankle swelling by evening.
- Home BP diary, last 2 weeks, mornings: average 146/92.
- Missed 2 doses in 6 weeks (forgot while travelling).
- No chest pain, no breathlessness, no visual symptoms, no palpitations.
- Non-smoker. Walks about 15 min most days. Eats a lot of canned and salted food.
- Family history: father had a stroke at 68.
- No known drug allergies.
- Today: BP 148/94, repeat 146/92 (seated, left arm). HR 76 regular. Weight 91 kg, height 176 cm, BMI 29.4.
- Trace bilateral ankle edema. Heart sounds normal. Chest clear.
- Baseline labs (2 months ago): creatinine 82 µmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, fasting glucose 5.4 mmol/L, LDL 3.6 mmol/L, urine ACR normal.
- Plan discussed: add losartan 50 mg once daily, keep amlodipine 5 mg, repeat creatinine and potassium in 2 weeks, reduce salt, keep the home BP diary, review in 4 weeks.
```

### Round A: one line {#round-a-no-template}

Open a new chat. Type this line, then paste the facts block under it.

<!-- paste: lab1-round-a | Lab 1, Round A: the one line -->
```text
Write a progress note for this patient.
```

Take the first draft. Do not re-prompt, and do not edit it. Keep it in its own chat, or paste it into a note under **A**.

### Round B: the four parts {#round-b-the-four-part-framework}

Open another new chat, so Round A cannot influence it. Paste this prompt, then paste the facts block under it. It fills the four parts (Role, Context, Format, Constraints) and points to that block, so there is nothing to edit.

<!-- paste: lab1-round-b | Lab 1, Round B: the four-part prompt -->
```text
ROLE: You are a primary care physician writing a progress note for the chart, for the next clinician who sees this patient.
CONTEXT: This is a follow-up visit for hypertension. Use ONLY the facts in the block headed CASE A at the end of this message. If something needed is missing, write [MISSING: what] instead of guessing.
FACTS:
See the block headed CASE A at the end of this message.
FORMAT: A SOAP note with exactly four headings, in this order: Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan. Short lines, as in a real chart. Maximum 150 words.
CONSTRAINTS: Do not add findings, doses, or diagnoses that are not in the facts. No hedging phrases. Copy every number and dose exactly as given, with the units given. Standard clinical abbreviations are fine.
```

Take the first draft and keep it in its own chat, or paste it into a note under **B**.

### Put them side by side: six checks {#six-checks}

Look at A and B side by side, with the card open. For each check, tick the draft if it passes. Compare against the facts, not against how the sentence sounds.

| The check | Draft A | Draft B |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Amlodipine 5 mg once daily | | |
| 2. Losartan 50 mg once daily, added | | |
| 3. Creatinine and potassium again in 2 weeks | | |
| 4. Review in 4 weeks | | |
| 5. Ankle swelling shown as new since amlodipine | | |
| 6. Nothing added that the card does not say | | |
| **Ticks out of 6** | | |

Check 6 is the one to read slowly: an extra finding, a dose or a diagnosis that is not on the card counts against the draft, however natural it reads.

Then type in the chat **A** or **B**: which draft would you sign with fewer changes? Add one sentence on what the change did. Your numbers are yours, and they will not match anyone else's. One run of one case is not a measurement of any tool.

What good looks like: both columns ticked, and one sentence on what the prompt changed for you. If both drafts pass all six, look at what else differs (length, order, how much was added) and say that.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Keep this
Change one thing, put the results side by side, and check against the source, not against the tone.
:::

## 2. Ask for what it cannot know [8 min]{.time} {#part-2}

**The one change: you ask for something the tool can only guess.** The aim is not to catch the tool out. It is to see, once and safely, how sure a wrong answer sounds, and how quickly a check settles it.

If your assistant lets you turn search or browsing off, turn it off for this part: it is about what the tool does from memory. Then paste this into a new chat, with a topic from your own field so that you can judge the answer.

<!-- paste: lab1-five-papers | Lab 1, part 2: ask for five papers -->
```text
List five papers on [a topic in your field], each with authors, journal, year and DOI.
```

If the tool declines, that is a good answer: note it. Then push once, as a busy colleague might: `I need the exact figure for my reference list. Give your best answer.`

### Look for the first paper

Read the list once. Notice how sure it sounds. Then take the **first** paper and search for its exact title (PubMed, Google Scholar or the journal's own site) for about two minutes. Mark what you found:

- **Found as written**: the title, authors, journal and year match.
- **Found, but a detail differs**: the paper exists, and the year, authors or journal are not what the list says.
- **Not found**: nothing matches.

Every one of the five is told in the same voice. Which exist is something only your search can tell you. If the first paper checks out, try the last one, and if all of them are real, say so: you checked, and that is a result too.

If you would rather, use another probe from your own field: the exact number and year of a national guideline, a percentage to one decimal place with the study's name, or the newest safety communication for a drug class you prescribe. Each has the same check: look for the one item the answer is sure about. Do not use a drug interaction, and never act on any of these answers.

### Run the check, then save it {#run-the-check-then-save-it}

Run the three questions on the answer:

1. Could I defend this to a colleague?
2. Does it point to something I can verify?
3. Would I catch it if it were wrong?

For question 2, you have just done it with the first paper. For question 3, ask whether you would have noticed had you not looked.

Save the answer in a note titled `lab1-practice-output`, with this exact line above it. [Lab 3](../day3/lab3-spot-the-error.qmd) reuses it, and a saved wrong answer must never pass for a right one.

<!-- paste: practice-output-line | The warning line above a saved practice output -->
```text
PRACTICE OUTPUT: CONTAINS DELIBERATELY UNRELIABLE CONTENT. NOT FOR CLINICAL USE.
```

Add one line under the answer: what you found for the paper you searched, and your verdict: trust, verify first, or discard.

What good looks like: one saved answer with the header line, one item you searched for, and a verdict.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Keep this
The tone told you nothing. Only the search did.
:::

## 3. One question, two ways of answering [5 min]{.time} {#part-3}

**The one change: where the answer comes from.** A general assistant writes from what it learned in training. The second option shows sources you can open: a literature-grounded tool, your assistant's search or citation mode, or a plain literature search. Use whichever you can open today. [Module 3](m3-choosing-tools.qmd#second-option) lists all three, and nothing here depends on one of them.

Choose a general clinical question from your own field, one you can judge, with no patient details. If nothing comes to mind, use this one, taken from [Case C](../reference/case-cards.qmd#case-c)'s question for cardiology: *In adults with newly diagnosed atrial fibrillation, what does the evidence say about rate control versus rhythm control?* Ask both the same question: your assistant in its tab, the second option in one more. For a plain literature search, type the question's key terms.

<!-- prompt: evidence-question | Evidence question with sources | Ask a general clinical question, with no patient details, and ask for sources you can open -->
```text
[A general clinical question from your own field.] Summarize the main options and how strong the evidence is for each. Cite sources I can open. If you cannot find a source, say so. This is a general question: no patient details.
```

### Look for one thing

For each answer, count the sources you could look up: a paper, a guideline or a link you could open. Then open one, and see whether it says what the sentence claims.

| | General assistant | Second option |
|---|---|---|
| Sources I could open (count) | | |

Then write one line: which would you trust, and for what? Type your two counts in the chat. This is one run of one question, not a benchmark. Do not conclude that one tool is better. Conclude what each lets you check.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Keep this
A source you can open is something you can check. A fluent answer with no source is not.
:::

## 4. Debrief [5 min]{.time} {#debrief}

Type in the chat the one prompt, or the one change to a prompt, that worked best today, and why. Two or three of you will then unmute and say more.

Then add it to your personal prompt library: a note on your phone or laptop, one entry per prompt.

```text
TITLE: [what it does, in a few words]
PROMPT: [the prompt, with [brackets] where the facts go]
CHECK: [what I verify in the output, every time]
```

The course's own collection is the [prompt library](../reference/prompt-library.qmd). Copy from it, change the facts, and keep your own version. Bring your favorite prompt to Day Two.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Keep this
Save the prompt that worked, together with the line you checked.
:::

## Worksheet

Copy this table into your notes and fill it in as you go.

| Where | What to record |
|---|---|
| Part 1, the two drafts | Ticks out of 6 for A and for B; A or B, and one sentence on what the change did |
| Part 2, the probe | The topic; the paper I searched for; found as written, found but different, or not found |
| Part 2, the check | Defend, verify, catch (yes or no each); verdict: trust, verify first, or discard |
| Part 3, one question, two answers | Sources I could open for each; which I would trust, and for what |
| Part 4, my library | The prompt I am keeping, and the line I check in its output |
